s01.text: Here is a thirteen-billion-parameter model. It is the kind of thing that runs on a rack of GPUs in a data centre.

s02.text: And here is what it weighs: twenty-six gigabytes of memory, just to hold the numbers.

s03.text: Your phone has eight gigabytes. So this is a problem.

s04.text: The first answer everyone reaches for is quantization: store the same numbers, more cheaply.

s05.text: Sixteen bits becomes eight. Eight becomes four. Four becomes two. Every halving is a free lunch.

s06.text: And then the ladder hits one bit. A weight is a yes, or a no. That is the floor people fight over.

s07.text: So what happens if you try to go below one bit? Because below one bit, there is no yes, and there is no no.

s08.text: Samsung's LittleBit starts by refusing the premise.

s09.text: It does not store smaller numbers. It does not round them down. It deletes them.

s10.text: A model's weights are matrices. Take one: four thousand rows by four thousand columns.

s11.text: That matrix is enormously redundant. It is not four thousand independent directions. It is a few.

s12.text: So factor it. The big matrix becomes A times B. A is tall and thin, B is short and wide, and the rank is small.

s13.text: Now the trick: binarize both factors. Every single entry in A, and every entry in B, becomes plus one, or minus one.

s14.text: Not small numbers. No decimals. No rounding. A sign.

s15.text: The original matrix was never stored. At run time you multiply A by B, and rebuild it.

s16.text: Which means the information was never in the weights to begin with. It was in the relationship between two sign matrices.

s17.text: So how do you get to a tenth of a bit per weight? You count differently.

s18.text: You are not storing sixteen bits per weight. You are storing two sign matrices, and asking what that costs per weight.

s19.text: For a thirteen-billion-parameter model at a small rank, the answer is about zero point one bits per weight.

s20.text: That number is an accounting measure. It is not a physical cell holding a tenth of a bit.

s21.text: Nothing in hardware stores a tenth of a bit. It is a way of counting what the model costs.

s22.text: Hold on to this: the model is not smaller because the numbers got smaller. It is smaller because most of the model was never numbers at all.

s23.text: Deleting the numbers has to cost something. It does.

s24.text: A sign throws away magnitude. A weight of plus zero point zero zero one, and a weight of plus ten, become the same plus one.

s25.text: Real weight matrices are not random noise. Their singular values fall off fast. A few directions carry most of the energy.

s26.text: This is the intuition from LittleBit two: for a spectrum like that, a low-rank binary approximation can beat a tiny-rank float one.

s27.text: So the question is not how much you keep. It is which directions you keep.

s28.text: So LittleBit adds a compensation term that learns the error across rows, across columns, and across the latent dimension.

s29.text: That is the part that recovers what the signs threw away.

s30.text: Even so, something was still wrong. And the reason was geometric.

s31.text: To multiply two matrices cheaply, you need their directions. The singular vectors of the latent space.

s32.text: And those vectors are spiky. Almost all of their energy sits in a few coordinates.

s33.text: Here is why that is the worst possible shape. A sign can only be plus one or minus one.

s34.text: And a spiky vector has almost all of its mass in a handful of coordinates. Quantize that, and those coordinates saturate.

s35.text: You gain nothing by being accurate where the vector barely points, and you lose everything by being wrong where it strongly points.

s36.text: LittleBit two calls it latent geometry misalignment. And it is a real bug, not a tuning problem.

s37.text: The fix is to rotate the latent space first, so the distribution is flat, and only then quantize it.

s38.text: They call it internal latent rotation, and they interleave it with the quantization itself.

s39.text: And the crucial part: the rotation folds into the factors. It costs nothing at inference time.

s40.text: So what does it buy? Memory: about thirty-one times less than full precision.

s41.text: Size: Llama two, thirteen billion parameters, in under zero point nine gigabytes.

s42.text: Quality: it matches the fidelity of leading one-bit baselines. At a tenth of their bits.

s43.text: Speed: the paper claims a potential eleven point six times inference speedup against sixteen-bit.

s44.text: Potential is the load-bearing word. There is no hardware that multiplies one-bit matrices that fast yet.

s45.text: And one number in this film is ours, not the paper's: twenty-six gigabytes down to zero point nine is a twenty-nine times drop in the model itself.

s46.text: That is just thirteen billion parameters, times sixteen bits.

s47.text: None of this is on your phone yet. And it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

s48.text: There are no sub-one-bit multiply kernels. The storage format does not exist. The bandwidth saving is theoretical until hardware catches up.

s49.text: What exists is a direction, and a result strong enough that people are now building toward it.

s50.text: There is a parallel road here. BitNet went the other way, to ternary weights: plus one, minus one, and zero.

s51.text: Both are asking the same question. What is the smallest amount of information a language model actually needs?

s52.text: Because that number is the whole budget. A model you cannot fit is a model you cannot run.

s53.text: And a model you can run on the device is the difference between a service, and a feature.

s54.text: So the layer below the layer. Not smaller numbers. Fewer numbers.

s55.text: A thirteen-billion-parameter model, factored into two sign matrices, rebuilt on the fly, at a tenth of a bit per weight.

s56.text: That is LittleBit, and LittleBit two. NeurIPS twenty twenty-five, and the follow-up this year.

s57.text: We made a sixty-second version too, if you want the short version.
